title: Non-redundant aperture masks for segmented mirrors
statement: A segmented telescope mirror with s rings of hexagonal segments around a missing central segment has 3s(s + 1) segments, centred at the points a + b*w of the triangular lattice (w = e^(i pi/3)) with hexagonal norm max(|a|, |b|, |a + b|) from 1 to s. An aperture mask that puts one hole on each of some segments is non-redundant when no baseline repeats: the vectors joining two holes are all different, a vector and its negative counting as the same baseline. Let h(s) be the largest number of holes of a non-redundant mask on the s-ring mirror. The headline cell is s = 10 (330 segments): find a non-redundant mask with more than 23 holes.
submission: Text file: one line 'a b' per hole, the segment a + b*w (hexagonal norm 1..10), each segment at most once.
score: the number of holes, an integer (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: local search that moves one hole at a time to the segment creating the fewest repeated baselines, with a tabu list (tools/src/nrm.c, mode ls)

context: Aperture masking turns a single telescope into an interferometer: a mask with a few small holes in the pupil plane makes every pair of holes a baseline, and when no baseline repeats (a non-redundant mask) each Fourier component of the image is measured by one pair only, so closure phases are free of redundancy noise (Haniff et al. 1987; Tuthill et al. 2000). On a segmented mirror the holes must avoid the gaps between segments, which in practice puts at most one hole on each segment, at its centre. The mask of the NIRISS instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope has 7 holes on 7 of the mirror's 18 segments (Sivaramakrishnan et al. 2023); our exhaustive search shows that 7 is the most possible on that layout (s = 2). Keck's and GTC's mirrors have the 36-segment layout s = 3, where the most is 9; HET and SALT have 91 segments, TMT 492 and ELT 798, and the question grows with them. Mathematically h(s) is the largest Sidon set (all differences distinct) inside a hexagon of the triangular lattice with its centre removed. Golay (1971) designed compact non-redundant arrays for radio and optical astronomy, Blackburn, Etzion, Martin and Paterson (2010) found the largest hexagonal-grid configurations with distinct differences whose points are at most a given distance apart (diameter up to 10), and Blackburn, Panoui, Paterson and Stinson (2010) classified honeycomb arrays; none of these fixes the region to a mirror's segment layout with the centre removed, and we found no table of h(s). Counting baselines gives h(10) <= 36; the gap between 23 and 36 is open, as is the growth of h(s).
references: C. A. Haniff, C. D. Mackay, D. J. Titterington, D. Sivia, J. E. Baldwin, The first images from optical aperture synthesis, Nature 328 (1987) 694-696
P. G. Tuthill, J. D. Monnier, W. C. Danchi, E. H. Wishnow, C. A. Haniff, Michelson interferometry with the Keck I telescope, Publ. Astron. Soc. Pacific 112 (2000) 555-565
A. Sivaramakrishnan et al., The James Webb Space Telescope Aperture Masking Interferometer, Publ. Astron. Soc. Pacific 135 (2023) 015003 (arXiv:2201.01524)
M. J. E. Golay, Point arrays having compact, nonredundant autocorrelations, J. Opt. Soc. Am. 61 (1971) 272-273

S. R. Blackburn, T. Etzion, K. M. Martin, M. B. Paterson, Two-dimensional patterns with distinct differences: constructions, bounds, and maximal anticodes, IEEE Trans. Inform. Theory 56 (2010) 1216-1229 (arXiv:0811.3832)
S. R. Blackburn, A. Panoui, M. B. Paterson, D. R. Stinson, Honeycomb arrays, Electron. J. Combin. 17 (2010) R172

novelty.verdict: new question: nobody asked for the largest non-redundant set of segments of a hexagonal segmented mirror with its centre removed. Masks are designed instrument by instrument, and distinct-difference configurations in the hexagonal grid were studied with a bound on their diameter, which is a different question.
closest: S. R. Blackburn, T. Etzion, K. M. Martin and M. B. Paterson (2010): the largest hexagonal-grid configurations with distinct differences and diameter at most r (r <= 10, by backtracking). Their region is any set of that diameter; here the region is fixed (the segment layout) and the centre is missing, as on real telescopes.
The JWST NIRISS mask (7 holes on 18 segments) and other masks designed instrument by instrument; none asks for the maximum on a given layout.
Golay arrays (1971) and honeycomb arrays (Blackburn, Panoui, Paterson, Stinson 2010): non-redundant arrays with other constraints (compactness; one dot in every row in three directions).
novelty.benchmark: the benchmark's families (covering designs, codes, covering arrays, schedules) have no aperture or Sidon-set family

first_values.note: Exact values from tools/src/nrm.c (mode max: depth-first search over segments with the baselines used so far marked); the local search (mode ls) reproduces them. Larger values are lower bounds.

baseline.text: 23 holes, held by Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: the mask in `refs/nrm-segments.txt` (253 baselines, all different). Counting baselines (the 630 baseline vectors of hexagonal norm at most 20, up to sign) gives h(10) <= 36.

bound.source: counting: the h(h - 1)/2 baselines of a mask with h holes are distinct vectors of hexagonal norm at most 20, of which there are 630 up to sign, so h(h - 1)/2 <= 630
